name: query_database
description: Run a single read-only SQL SELECT query against the sample_superstore SQLite database. Use ONLY for metrics not covered by the other tools (e.g. order count, profit breakdowns, customer/category lookups, year-over-year or other period-over-period comparisons). Prefer get_revenue for revenue and get_active_users for active users. For period-over-period questions (e.g. "which category grew the most each year"), do the actual comparison inside the SQL itself — e.g. window functions like LAG() to get the prior period's value per group, then rank within each period — and return one row per period with the answer, rather than dumping raw per-period-per-group totals and leaving the comparison for the reader to do by eye. When the result has more than one row, the app already renders it as a table — don't restate every row in text, just summarize the finding.

sql.description: A single SELECT statement, valid SQLite syntax.

name: get_revenue
description: Get total revenue (sum) for a given date range, optionally filtered by region/category.

region.description: Optional exact region name to filter by

category.description: Optional exact category name to filter by

name: get_chart_data
description: Get a metric broken down by a dimension (e.g. revenue by month, profit by category), suitable for rendering as a chart. Use this whenever the user asks to see/plot/chart/visualize a trend or a breakdown, instead of a single number.

metric.description: revenue = SUM(sales), profit = SUM(profit), orders = COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), quantity = SUM(quantity) (units sold), returned_revenue = sales belonging to orders that were later returned. cost = sales minus profit — use this for any question about costs, and say in your answer that it is defined that way, because the database has NO cost column: `sales` is already net of discount, so this figure lumps cost of goods, discounts and everything else together and can never show that a loss was caused by discounting specifically (compare discount_rate for that). Derived (ratio) metrics, not summable totals: revenue_per_order = revenue / orders (a.k.a. average order value / AOV), profit_margin = profit / revenue (a fraction, e.g. 0.15 for 15%), discount_rate = average discount applied (a fraction), return_rate = share of orders that were returned (a fraction), delivery_days = average calendar days from order_date to ship_date (use this for any question about shipping/delivery/fulfillment speed).

group_by.description: Dimension to break the metric down by. day/week/month/quarter/year are time buckets on order_date and render as a trend line (week is labeled by its Monday); region, state (US state/province), category, sub_category, segment (Consumer/Corporate/Home Office), and ship_mode (Standard Class/Second Class/First Class/Same Day) render as a bar chart. Pick the coarsest time bucket that answers the question — group_by=day over a multi-year range returns hundreds of points.

region.description: Optional exact region name to filter by

category.description: Optional exact category name to filter by

name: get_active_users
description: Get the number of distinct/unique active users for a given date range. This is a non-additive metric — always computed as COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) over the full requested range, never summed from smaller periods.

name: generate_report
description: Generate a dashboard-style report for a date range: revenue/profit/orders KPIs compared against the immediately preceding period of the same length (always shown, regardless of `metric`), plus a monthly trend, a breakdown by category and region, and a top-5 sub-categories table — all three driven by `metric`. Use this when the user asks for a dashboard, summary report, or overview of the business for a period — not for a single-metric question, which should use get_revenue/get_active_users/get_chart_data instead.

region.description: Optional exact region name to filter by

category.description: Optional exact category name to filter by

metric.description: Which metric drives the monthly trend, category/region breakdown, and top sub-categories table. Defaults to revenue. Options: revenue, profit, orders, quantity (units sold), cost (sales minus profit — the database has no cost column, see get_chart_data for the caveat), revenue_per_order (a.k.a. average order value / AOV), profit_margin (profit as a % of revenue), discount_rate (average discount applied, as a %), return_rate (share of orders returned, as a %), returned_revenue (sales in orders that were returned), delivery_days (average days from order to shipment). Use this to rebuild the dashboard around a different metric — e.g. metric=orders for order volume, or metric=profit_margin when the user asks about margins rather than totals. The KPI row itself always shows revenue, profit, and orders together no matter what's picked here.

name: get_cohort_retention
description: Get cohort retention for customers: each customer's cohort is the calendar day, week, month, quarter, or year of their first order within the given date range, and for each following period it reports what percentage of that cohort placed at least one more order. Use this for any retention/cohort analysis question, instead of query_database or code_execution.
